settings.editor:
If your shower suddenly feels more like a drizzle than a shower, you’re not imagining things.

Low water pressure is one of the most common plumbing issues homeowners deal with across Springfield, Hendersonville, White House, and surrounding Middle Tennessee communities. 

Sometimes the fix is simple, like clearing buildup from a showerhead. Other times, low pressure can point to a larger plumbing issue, such as a hidden leak, failing pressure regulator, or aging pipes.

The good news is that most water pressure problems come down to a few common causes. Here’s what may be behind the issue and what to do next.

settings.title: Quick Answer: What Causes Low Water Pressure in a House?

settings.editor:
Low water pressure in a house is usually caused by clogged fixtures, partially closed shutoff valves, hidden plumbing leaks, failing pressure regulators, or aging pipes that restrict water flow. 

If multiple fixtures are affected, the issue may involve the home’s main plumbing system.

settings.title: What Is Considered Low Water Pressure?

settings.editor:
Most homes operate best between 45 and 60 PSI (pounds per square inch).

If your faucets feel weak, showers lose pressure easily, or multiple fixtures struggle at once, your water pressure may be too low.

Common signs include:

  • Weak shower pressure
  • Slow-filling sinks or tubs
  • Appliances taking longer to run
  • Water pressure dropping when multiple fixtures are used
Before assuming the problem is something major, it’s worth checking a few of the most common causes first. Some water pressure issues are surprisingly simple to identify and fix.

settings.title: 1. A Shutoff Valve May Not Be Fully Open

settings.editor:
Your home has shutoff valves that control water flow throughout the plumbing system. If the main valve or water meter valve is only partially open, it can reduce pressure across the house.

This sometimes happens after:

  • Plumbing repairs
  • Water heater installation
  • Routine maintenance
  • Someone accidentally adjusting the valve
When a valve isn’t fully open, water can still flow, just not at the pressure you’re used to.

settings.title: Signs This May Be the Problem

settings.editor:
• Weak pressure throughout the house
  • Low pressure at both hot and cold fixtures
  • Pressure that stays consistently weak
If you know where the main shutoff valve is, check whether it’s fully open. If you’re unsure, it’s best to have a plumber inspect it rather than force the valve and risk damage.

settings.title: 2. Mineral Buildup Is Restricting Water Flow

settings.editor:
If the low pressure is only happening in one sink or shower, buildup inside the fixture is a likely culprit.

Over time, minerals in the water can collect inside faucet aerators and showerheads, restricting water flow and making pressure feel weaker.

This is especially common in:

  • Bathroom sinks
  • Kitchen faucets
  • Showerheads

• One fixture is weaker than the others
  • Water sprays unevenly
  • Pressure slowly gets worse over time

Try removing and cleaning the aerator or showerhead. If the issue improves, buildup was likely the problem.

In some homes, recurring buildup may also point to water quality issues that should be addressed long-term.

settings.title: 3. Your Pressure Regulator Could Be Failing

settings.editor:
Not every home has a pressure regulator, but when one starts failing, the symptoms are usually noticeable.

A pressure regulator controls the water pressure entering your home. When it malfunctions, pressure may suddenly become too weak, or fluctuate throughout the day.

settings.title: Signs of a Bad Pressure Regulator

settings.editor:
• Sudden pressure drop throughout the house
  • Pressure changes at different times of day
  • Weak showers and slow faucets across multiple rooms
Because this affects the entire plumbing system, it usually requires professional testing to confirm.
If low pressure showed up suddenly throughout the home, a pressure regulator issue is worth investigating before the problem worsens.

settings.title: 4. You May Have a Hidden Plumbing Leak

settings.editor:
This is the issue most homeowners worry about—and for good reason.

Leaks inside walls, crawl spaces, underground lines, or ceilings can reduce water pressure by allowing water to escape before it reaches your fixtures.

In many Middle Tennessee homes, especially older ones with crawl spaces, these leaks can go unnoticed longer than expected.

settings.title: Signs You May Have a Leak

settings.editor:
• Higher water bills
  • Damp spots or musty smells
  • Soft flooring or water stains
  • The sound of running water when nothing is on
  • Pressure loss in multiple fixtures
Small leaks rarely stay small. In many cases, a professional pipe and leak repair is needed to stop the pressure loss and prevent water damage.

settings.title: 5. Older Pipes May Be Restricting Water Flow

settings.editor:
In some homes, the issue isn’t a fixture or valve—it’s the plumbing pipes themselves.

Older pipes can corrode, narrow internally, or collect buildup over time. As the inside of the pipe becomes more restricted, less water can move through.

This is especially common in older homes with aging galvanized plumbing.

settings.title: Signs of Aging or Corroded Pipes

settings.editor:
• Pressure that gradually worsens over time
  • Multiple fixtures affected
  • Occasional discolored water
  • Frequent plumbing repairs
This type of issue usually develops slowly, which is why many homeowners don’t notice how much pressure they’ve lost until the problem becomes more obvious.

settings.title: When Low Water Pressure Is Probably Not a DIY Fix

settings.editor:
There’s nothing wrong with cleaning a showerhead or checking a shutoff valve.

But if the low pressure:

  • Appeared suddenly
  • Is affecting multiple fixtures
  • Came with higher water bills
  • Keeps getting worse over time

…it’s smart time to call a plumber to handle it.

What seems like a small inconvenience can sometimes point to a hidden leak, failing regulator, or pipe problem that becomes much more expensive if ignored.

settings.title: Frequently Asked Questions About Low Water Pressure

items.item_title: What is considered normal water pressure for a house?
Can low water pressure increase my utility bill?
Why is my water pressure worse upstairs?
Does hard water cause low water pressure?
Is low water pressure more common in older homes?
Can low water pressure fix itself?

settings.editor: Most homes operate best between 45 and 60 PSI (pounds per square inch). Pressure below that range may feel weak at showers, sinks, and appliances.
Yes, depending on the cause. Hidden leaks are one of the most common reasons low pressure and higher water bills happen at the same time.
Gravity naturally affects water flow, so low pressure is often more noticeable on upper floors. Pipe restrictions or pressure regulator issues can make the problem worse.
It can. Hard water leaves behind mineral deposits that build up inside pipes, faucets, and showerheads, restricting water flow over time.
Yes. Older homes often have aging plumbing systems, corroded pipes, or outdated fixtures that can restrict water flow and reduce pressure.
Usually not. While temporary supply issues can sometimes improve on their own, most ongoing pressure problems continue getting worse until the underlying cause is addressed.
